earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog lists only Ethnologue 16 and Meek 1931 notes/wordlist; no grammar or phonology of Kofa located.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Kofa language' (redirects to 'Bata language'); cites Ethnologue 25, Blench 2019 Atlas of Nigerian Languages 4th ed., ALCAM 2012, Boyd 2002
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone; only consonant/vowel inventories from Boyd 2002. Lists kso as an 'individual code' under Bata but does not assign Kofa to a dialect.

sources.citation: Gravina, Richard. 2014. The Phonology of Proto-Central Chadic. Utrecht: LOT (LOT 375). Section 6.3 'Bata group', pp. 144-151 (6.3.3 'Bata and Bachama', p. 146)
sources.note: Silent on stress for Bata/Kofa. Explicitly excludes it: 'The result is a reconstruction of the sound system of Proto-Central Chadic (though not including tone or stress)' (p. 1 area, line 777 of text) and '(No attempt has been made to reconstruct tone or stress.)' (section 8 intro). The Bata group section treats vowels, prosodies, labialized/palatalized consonants only.

sources.citation: Lewis, M. Paul (ed.). 2009. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 16th ed. Dallas: SIL International. Entry 'Kofa' (kso). (Wayback Machine capture 2012 of ethnologue.com/show_language.asp?code=kso)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or phonology. Population 1,100 (2003); Adamawa State, Song LGA, north of Belul road, north of Yola; alternate name Kota; 'Reportedly a separate language from Bura-Pabir [bwr]'; classification Afro-Asiatic, Chadic, Biu-Mandara, A, A.2, 1.

sources.citation: Boyd, Raymond. 2002. Bata phonology: a reappraisal. Munich: LINCOM Europa. 60 pp. — corrected glossary extract (pp. 54-58) posted by the author at rblanguesdafrique.info
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: HathiTrust digitized, search-only (in copyright); interlibrary loan
sources.note: The glossary extract has no mention of stress, accent or tone marking; its prefatory note concerns consonant/vowel 'prosodies' (palatal, labial) in the orthography only. The full 60-page book (which would hold any stress/tone statement) is not open; Glottolog 5.3 attaches it to Bacama [bcy] on Blench's p.c. that the data are 'mostly Bacama'.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid record kofa1236 'Kofa' [kso], Bookkeeping, with Ethnologue comment of type 'spurious'
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Identity note: "It is correct that it is distinct from Bura-Pabir [bwr] but already hh:hew:Meek:Tribal:I:118-121 had data from Kofa and shows that they speak the same language as Malabu, i.e., Bata [bta]." Only ref attached is Ethnologue 16 (med type wordlist_or_less).

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 registration authority record for kso 'Kofa'
sources.note: Nothing; code is Active, individual, living; no change request listed (i.e. the code has not been retired despite Glottolog's spurious verdict).
Nothing on phonology; has a 'said to be the same as' Q56254 (Bata) statement.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2019. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages, 4th ed. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation (Bata / Kofa entries)
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.access_detail: open copy online, not fetched sources
sources.note: Gives the current Nigerian-side identification of 'Kofa' (Wikipedia cites it for the kso = Bata listing); useful for the identity note, not for a stress statement.

sources.citation: Rueck, Michael J., Carol Magnusson & Yakubu Oro. 2008. Bwatiye Sociolinguistic Survey Draft. SIL Nigeria. 31 pp. (Glottolog ref 682037)
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: SIL survey of the Bata/Bacama area; could settle which village varieties (incl. Kofa) belong to Bata and might carry a short phonology note.

sources.citation: Pweddon, Nicholas Nzovudetho (with Neil Skinner). 2001. Bwatiye-English Dictionary, with English-Bwatiye index. Jos: Midland Press. xi+188 pp.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: A modern dictionary of Bacama/Bwatiye; the introduction would state how tone/stress is marked in headwords.

sources.citation: Carnochan, Jack. 1972. Pitch, tone and intonation in Bachama. Phonetica Pragensia 3: 59-63; and Carnochan, Jack. 1970. Categories of the verbal piece in Bachama. African Language Studies 11: 81-112
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.access_detail: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: The closest published prosodic description in the Bata/Bacama cluster (Bacama is 'often considered the same language' as Bata); a five-page paper on pitch, tone and intonation is exactly where a stress-vs-tone statement would sit.

sources.citation: Meek, Charles Kingsley. 1931. Tribal Studies in Northern Nigeria, vol. I, pp. 118-121 (Kofa notes and wordlist, in the chapter on the Bata-speaking peoples: Zumu/Jimo, Bulai, Malabu, Kofa, Muleng, Bolki...). London: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: The only primary data on Kofa itself; the source Glottolog uses to identify Kofa with Malabu/Bata. Ethnographic notes plus wordlist, so at most a remark on accent in the transcription, but it is the sole Kofa-specific document.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2019 (and earlier eds.). An Atlas of Nigerian Languages. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation
sources.note: Not opened: rogerblench.info serves a captcha, the nairametrics mirror returns HTML, academia.edu requires login. Would give only the Kofa = Bata-dialect identification, not a stress statement.
